Three-way summit in Shenzhen: Xi greets Trump on the tarmac after pledging with Putin to “lead” a multipolar world, Washington expects “no agreement”

On Thursday, November 19, Xi Jinping brings together Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of APEC, for a first three-way summit. The day before, Xi greeted Trump in person at the airport and, together with Putin, called for a “multipolar” world. On the agenda: nuclear weapons, Iran, Ukraine, but Washington expects no agreement [1][2][3][4].

Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, November 18, at 4:42 p.m., and Xi Jinping was waiting for him on the tarmac himself, a gesture returning the airport welcome Trump gave Xi in September [6][2].

Earlier on Wednesday, Xi received Vladimir Putin: China and Russia must “lead and advance the trend toward a multipolar world,” he said [4]. Putin denounced sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions [5].

On Thursday, Trump and Xi were first due to hold a one-on-one meeting followed by a working lunch, before Putin joined them [10]. It is the first three-way meeting between the leaders of the three biggest military powers [9].

The White House says Trump wants to discuss the war with Iran and a possible three-way deal on nuclear weapons [2]. “We don’t expect to reach any kind of agreement,” warns a senior U.S. official, who describes the summit as “the first conversation” [3].
Ukraine is not officially on the agenda: Xi considers it a European matter [2]. A Kremlin adviser, on the contrary, says the talks will build on efforts toward a negotiated settlement of the war [9].

On trade, Washington and Beijing will not announce any new progress on their “Board of Trade,” which is meant to cut tariffs on $30bn worth of goods on each side, according to Reuters [7]. The trade truce runs until January 10, 2027 [8].

Key takeaway: this is the very first three-way meeting between the leaders of the world’s three biggest military powers [9]. Even without a deal, Washington presents opening a three-way discussion on nuclear weapons as an “entry point” [3].

Each is pursuing its own interest: Xi wants to show that China has become the country that brings others together, Putin gets a major global stage despite the war in Ukraine, and Trump wants to prove he can deal with both rivals [2].

The chip issue weighs on the meeting: the prospect of new U.S. restrictions on AI chips sold to China is expected to overshadow the talks, according to Reuters, a few days after the resignation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang [7]. The two countries are nonetheless due to discuss AI safety, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said [7].
For Beijing and Moscow, the message is clear: they present themselves as a tandem facing Washington, jointly denouncing protectionism just before Trump’s arrival [4][5].

If the three powers reach even a little common ground, even just on the principle of talking about nuclear weapons or Iran, it could calm oil prices and markets, and therefore your bills and your savings. Conversely, a new fight over chips or tariffs would make the electronics you buy more expensive.

Hormuz: an Emirati ship hit, one sailor missing and 11 injured, Iran pounds Kuwait and Bahrain, yet Brent slips toward $92

On Wednesday, November 18, Iran targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait and fired several times at Bahrain, in retaliation for a U.S. strike the day before. A ship belonging to the Emirati company Adnoc was hit in Hormuz: one sailor is missing and 11 are injured. Oil, however, is falling: Brent was at $92.12 on Thursday morning [1][3][4].

On Wednesday, the Iranian army said it had used drones to target Patriot air-defense batteries and launchers at the Ali Al Salem base in Kuwait [1][2]. The Kuwaiti army says it intercepted them, with no immediate damage [1]. It is the first Iranian attack on Kuwait since September [2].
Bahrain, home to the U.S. Fifth Fleet, intercepted several attacks, the third wave in a week [1][2]. Washington says no U.S. soldiers were injured [2].

These attacks respond to Tuesday’s U.S. strike on a missile launch site on Qeshm Island, which a U.S. official presented as retaliation for attacks on American troops [2]. According to the AP news agency, Ali Al Salem has already been hit at least 30 times since the start of the war [1].

On Tuesday evening, a ship operated by Adnoc Logistics & Services, a subsidiary of Abu Dhabi’s state oil company, was hit while crossing the strait: one crew member is missing, 11 are injured and the others were evacuated [3]. The company did not say who attacked it [3]. The Iranian navy, for its part, claims that three tankers were disabled by mines east of the strait [4].

Brent nevertheless fell 1.3% on Wednesday [4], weighed down by U.S. crude inventories that rose by 5.28 million barrels in a week, according to the API industry group, when Reuters had expected a decline [5][6]. At 2:37 GMT on Thursday, it stood at $92.12, and U.S. WTI crude at $83.17 [4].

Key takeaway: the war is flaring up again in the Gulf, but oil is no longer panicking. The International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts a surplus as early as this quarter, as Middle Eastern exports are recovering faster than demand [4]. Under U.S. protection, crude flows through Hormuz are said to have returned close to pre-war levels [4][1].

Goldman Sachs expects a surplus of about 2 million barrels per day in 2027 and Brent averaging $88 next year [4]. The prospect of a Fed rate hike in December is strengthening the dollar and also holding oil back [4]. Brent nonetheless remains far above its pre-war level of around $72 in late February [7].

Reserves have shrunk: the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, as part of a 172-million-barrel drawdown agreement [4]. And diplomacy is stalled as the war enters its ninth month [2].
For the Gulf, the bill is mounting: insurer Allianz Trade puts the damage at more than $200bn and lost revenue at $790bn by 2030 [8].

Oil falling despite the fighting gives you a bit of relief at the pump. But every ship hit in Hormuz is a reminder that prices can shoot back up within days: your fuel and heating oil still hinge on this strait.

Ukraine: Brussels revives joint debt with a €45bn loan, four countries say no, on the day Trump’s envoys arrive in Berlin

On Wednesday, November 18, the European Commission proposed lending Ukraine €45bn for 2027, financed by joint borrowing by the 27 member states. Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Bulgaria refuse to pay. On Thursday, November 19, Europeans, Ukrainians and Americans meet in Berlin [1][2][4][5].

The loan would cover about two-thirds of the €70bn gap in Ukraine’s 2027 budget: up to €25bn for the military and up to €20bn for the state budget [1]. The final third is expected from other allies, such as the United Kingdom, Norway, Canada and Japan [1].

The money would come from “Eurobonds,” debt issued by the EU on behalf of all members: member states would pay the interest each year [1]. Kyiv would only repay the principal once Russia has paid war reparations [1][2].

Slovakia’s Robert Fico warned that his country “will not take part” in a new loan: “We have done enough” [1][4]. The Czech Republic’s Andrej Babiš refuses to have his country act as guarantor, and Hungary’s Péter Magyar rejects any obligation to lend [1][4].
Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission, says she is “very confident” that all 27 will follow [2][3]. Yet this arrangement requires the agreement of every government [1].

In Berlin, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s envoys, are due to meet the Ukrainians and a new eight-member European negotiating team [5]. On the agenda: post-war security guarantees, an economic reconstruction plan and preparations for the next round of negotiations [5].
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is also hosting, with Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the “coalition of the willing,” nearly 40 delegations, at the Chancellery [6][7].

Key takeaway: Europe must now finance a large share of Ukraine’s effort on its own, and it is divided over the bill. The €45bn loan comes on top of the €90bn loan decided in December 2025, also through joint debt [1].

That precedent shows how Brussels gets around refusals: lacking unanimity, the €90bn loan was adopted through “enhanced cooperation,” a procedure that lets a group of countries move ahead without the others; the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia did not take part [3]. The Commission does not say whether the holdouts would be exempted again [1].

In Berlin, a new European team of eight negotiators is expected to face the Americans [5], while Moscow continues to refuse European participation in the negotiations [5][6]. A U.S. official speaks of a “coordinated diplomatic effort” alongside Trump’s trip to China [5].

France would pay its share of the interest on this joint debt, so indirectly through your taxes. But for Paris and Berlin, letting Ukraine run out of money would cost more: a defeat for Kyiv would weigh on the security and energy of all of Europe.

Social unrest: barred from striking, about a thousand CRS riot police call in sick, and Alliance union officers protest outside the Interior Ministry over their risk bonus

On Tuesday, November 17, about a thousand CRS riot police officers, who do not have the right to strike, went to see their doctor, leaving several cities without a crowd-control unit. On Wednesday, November 18, dozens of officers from the Alliance union gathered outside the Interior Ministry to demand a 35% risk bonus [1][4][6].

According to the Un1té union, nearly 1,000 CRS officers saw a doctor on Tuesday to get sick leave; the website Actu17 puts the figure at nearly 1,200, based on an internal count [6][5]. Between about twenty and thirty companies were affected, depending on the count [5][6].

In Marseille, no unit was available for crowd control on Tuesday; in the Var department, 64 of the 73 officers in Company 59 were absent [8]. The Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture says it “readjusted” its deployment [8].
Late Wednesday morning, several dozen Alliance officers protested on Place Beauvau in Paris [1][2]. Their secretary general, Fabien Vanhemelryck, was received by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez [2].

Alliance wants to raise the special duty allowance, the “risk bonus,” from 28.5% to 35% of base salary [3]. On November 13, Laurent Nuñez proposed gradually raising it to 33.5% by 2029, with a first step in April 2027 [4].
The unions consider this offer “insufficient,” even “unacceptable” [4]. The ministry promises a “letter of commitment” to confirm its new agreement [2].
Un1té denounces a “major wave of exhaustion and anger” [7]. Alliance is calling for a new national day of action on Thursday, November 26 [3].

Key takeaway: social anger is spreading to those tasked with containing it. The CRS, deployed for weeks against student and social protests, are exhausted, and sick leave serves as a disguised strike [4][6][1].

Why now? In its draft 2027 budget, the government is refusing a general pay rise for civil servants for the fourth year in a row, offering only eight additional index points to the lowest-paid employees [9]. Just on Tuesday, more than 100,000 people marched across France over public-sector pay [9].

The government is caught in a bind: giving in to the police would cost money when the budget is already fragile, and could revive demands from other civil servants. Not giving in risks a shortage of law enforcement if the protests continue. The government is due to meet the public-sector unions again after the December 11 workplace elections [9].

If you live in a big city, you may see fewer police officers at protests, and more tension. And every bonus increase granted weighs on the state budget, and therefore on taxes or on savings demanded elsewhere.

news.2026-11-19-anthropic-ipo-record.tit: Anthropic prices at $83 and raises $81bn: the biggest IPO in history, ahead of its Nasdaq debut this Thursday
news.2026-11-19-anthropic-ipo-record.sum: On Wednesday evening, November 18, Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude, priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the expected range. The offering raises about $81.3bn, a record ahead of SpaceX, and values the group at $1,500bn. Trading begins Thursday on the Nasdaq [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-19-anthropic-ipo-record.poi: The $83 price exceeds the $70 to $78 range announced in early November [2][4]. Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, compared with 825 million initially planned [5][4].

With about $81.3bn raised, the offering beats the record set by SpaceX, which raised about $75bn in June [1][2]. According to CNN, adding $26bn invested separately by tech giants such as Nvidia, the total reaches $107.3bn [6].

This private placement, meaning shares sold directly to a few large investors, brings together seven companies, including Nvidia, Google and Microsoft [4]. Nvidia alone is due to buy $10bn worth of shares [7].
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, along with about twenty other banks [8][9]. The stock will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT starting Thursday, November 19 [3][2].

On the financial side, Anthropic posted $33.24bn in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, about 1,200% more than a year earlier [5][10]. Its annualized revenue run rate reached about $81bn at the end of October [10].

But the net loss reached $104bn over the same period, mainly due to accounting entries tied to the value of its convertible bonds (loans that can be converted into shares), with no actual cash outflow [10][5].
CEO Dario Amodei owns about 1.3% of the company; his fortune is estimated at $19.8bn at the IPO price, according to Forbes [11].
news.2026-11-19-anthropic-ipo-record.why: Key takeaway: no company has ever raised so much money going public [1]. Pricing above the range shows that large investors are still willing to pay a premium for AI, even as Wall Street has been doubtful for weeks [2][12].

The backdrop is tense: on Wednesday, the S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight session and Nvidia lost nearly 3% despite record results [12]. The tech-heavy Nasdaq still gained 0.42%, lifted by anticipation around Anthropic [12].

An IPO is when a company sells its shares to the public for the first time. The price is set the day before with large investors; from Thursday, buying and selling on the Nasdaq will determine the share price [3].
news.2026-11-19-anthropic-ipo-record.for: If you hold a U.S. or “world” index fund in your stock savings plan or life-insurance savings, Nvidia, Google and Microsoft, which are investing in Anthropic, already carry a lot of weight in it. And a brand-new stock can swing sharply in its first days, in either direction: be careful before giving in to temptation.

news.2026-11-19-senat-budget-secu-2027.t: Social Security budget: the Senate adopts its version and protects pensions above €1,260, at the cost of a larger deficit
news.2026-11-19-senat-budget-secu-2027.s: On Wednesday, November 18, the French Senate adopted the 2027 Social Security budget at first reading, by 201 votes to 124. Senators scrapped the freeze on pensions above €1,260. Their version projects a €14bn deficit, compared with the €12.7bn targeted by the government [1][3][4].
news.2026-11-19-senat-budget-secu-2027.p: The vote took place on Wednesday, November 18: 201 in favor, 124 against and 15 abstentions [1][3]. The National Assembly had rejected the bill on October 23, so senators started again from the government’s original draft [3][4].

Main change: the Senate rejected the de-indexation of pensions above €1,260, meaning they would not be raised in line with inflation [1][2]. It voted for full indexation of pensions to prices in 2027 [3].

As a result, the Social Security deficit would reach €14bn in 2027 under the Senate’s version, €1.3bn more than the government’s target [3][4]. The government wants to bring it down from €21.8bn in 2026 to €12.7bn in 2027 [1].

For healthcare, the government is counting on €5.1bn in additional savings [4]. Health Minister Stéphanie Rist acknowledged before the senators that she had backtracked on a commitment: the cap on medical deductibles was raised this summer from €50 to €70 by decree [1].

Deputies and senators will meet on November 26 in a joint committee, seven deputies and seven senators tasked with finding a common text [3][4]. Parliament has until that date to adopt this budget, and until December 17 for the state budget [1].

The state budget comes before the Senate from November 20 to December 9 [6]. The general rapporteur, Christine Lavarde (LR), considers the government’s assumptions “very optimistic” and believes that “a recession cannot be ruled out” [5][6].
news.2026-11-19-senat-budget-secu-2027.w: Key takeaway: the Senate makes the budget more generous for retirees but widens the Social Security deficit. This is only one step: the final text will depend on an agreement with the National Assembly, where the government has no majority [3][4].

If no agreement is reached, the government could use Article 49.3, which adopts a bill without a vote unless a no-confidence motion passes, or ordinances if the timetable requires it [4]. Sébastien Lecornu rejects a “special law” that would simply roll over the 2026 appropriations [6].

The government does not want to go back on the compromise reached in autumn 2025 with the Socialist Party [4]. The Senate, for its part, has set itself the goal of keeping the public deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027 [6].
news.2026-11-19-senat-budget-secu-2027.f: If you are retired with a pension above €1,260, the Senate’s version guarantees you an increase in line with inflation in 2027, but nothing is final yet. And the cap on medical deductibles, what you pay on your boxes of medicine and doctor visits, is already rising to €70 a year.

news.2026-11-19-fed-compte-rendu-waller-: Fed: almost all officials want to raise rates in December, Christopher Waller talks of “shocking” with a half-point, and UnitedHealth plunges 10% on Wall Street

The minutes of the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) October meeting, released on Wednesday, November 18, show that almost all its officials expect a rate hike in December. Governor Christopher Waller is even arguing for a half-point. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight session, dragged down by insurer UnitedHealth [1][2][3].

Almost all Fed officials believe the policy rate will need to be raised by a quarter point in December, and two mentioned a half-point, according to the minutes [1]. According to Bloomberg, almost all believe further hikes will likely be needed to bring inflation back to 2% [4].

A “large majority” of the 19 officials fear inflation will persist, even as gasoline prices fall and the effects of tariffs and AI investment fade [5]. In October, the Fed held its rate between 3.75% and 4%, by 10 votes to 2 [6], after its first hike in more than three years in September [2].

On CNBC, Christopher Waller said a half-point hike is “probably” needed at the December 8-9 meeting: “You may need to, sort of, shock people” [2]. He is worried about companies getting used to 3% annual inflation [2].

A quarter point would be enough, in his view, if it comes with a clear signal of another hike in January [2]. New York Fed President John Williams rules out a giant hike: “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action” [7][8].

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 lost 0.23% to 7,323.63 points, its fifth straight decline, the longest losing streak since June [3]. The Dow Jones fell 1.11% to 50,198.17 points, while the Nasdaq gained 0.42% [3][9].

UnitedHealth, the U.S. health insurance giant, fell about 10% to $349.91, amid rising medical costs and pressure on margins [9][10]. It was already down more than 7% at midday [11]. Nvidia fell nearly 3% despite record results [9].

Key takeaway: the Fed, the U.S. central bank, is preparing to raise rates again to curb inflation, and the debate is now about the size of the hike [1][2]. Futures markets already fully price in a quarter point in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool [2].
The minutes also reveal a new concern: the effect of AI on inflation, CNBC notes [6]. For John Williams, AI is even the most likely source of persistent inflation [7][8].
UnitedHealth’s fall shows that the nervousness is not limited to tech: the group was the biggest drag on the Dow Jones on Wednesday [3].

U.S. interest rates call the shots on global markets: a more hawkish Fed draws capital toward the dollar and weighs on the stocks in your stock savings plan or life-insurance savings. If you are planning a trip to the United States, a stronger dollar also makes your stay more expensive.
